prompt.context_jp: 画面の中の茂木の脚に、明らかな乱れ___生じ始めた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 明らかな乱れ___生じ始めた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits this suddenly emerging detail.

feedback.correct_en: 乱れ is brand-new information the camera is revealing — the viewer wasn't tracking this disturbance before. が spotlights the emergence of a new element in the scene.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat 乱れ as an already-known topic, which contradicts the fact that this is the first moment the disturbance appears.

contrast_examples.jp: 乱れが生じた。
contrast_examples.en: A disturbance arose (new event).

contrast_examples.jp: その乱れは次第に大きくなった。
contrast_examples.en: That disturbance (already known) gradually grew.

prompt.context_jp: 先頭のケニア勢との差___、じりじりと縮まっていく。
prompt.prompt_jp: 先頭のケニア勢との差___じりじりと縮まっていく。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for this live-commentary observation.

feedback.correct_en: This is a live, dynamic event the narrator notices unfolding — the gap closing is new, focal information. が marks the subject of this emerging change.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame 差 as an established topic ('as for the gap...'), losing the sense of real-time discovery. を is wrong because 縮まる is intransitive.

contrast_examples.jp: 差がどんどん縮まる。
contrast_examples.en: The gap is closing (unfolding event).

contrast_examples.jp: その差はもう縮まらない。
contrast_examples.en: That gap (topic) won't close anymore.

prompt.context_jp: だが、その直後だった。茂木の脚___ふいに崩れ、沿道の柵に手をつくようにして倒れ込んだ。
prompt.prompt_jp: 茂木の脚___ふいに崩れ…
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for this sudden event.

feedback.correct_en: ふいに signals a sudden, newly-occurring event. が highlights 脚 as the focal subject of this unexpected collapse — the drama lies in the moment of occurrence.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat 脚 as an established topic, flattening the sudden-event feeling. Narrative beats like 'and then — his legs gave way!' naturally take が.

contrast_examples.jp: 脚が崩れた。
contrast_examples.en: His legs gave way (sudden event).

contrast_examples.jp: 脚はもう動かなかった。
contrast_examples.en: His legs (as topic) no longer moved.

prompt.context_jp: それでも茂木___諦めなかった。
prompt.prompt_jp: それでも茂木___諦めなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle expressing continuity of Mogi as the subject under discussion.

feedback.correct_en: The narration has been tracking Mogi for many lines; he is the established topic. は signals 'as for Mogi — despite everything, he didn't give up,' linking back to the ongoing theme.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would reintroduce Mogi as new information, which jars with それでも ('even so'), a connector that assumes we're still on him.

contrast_examples.jp: 茂木は諦めなかった。
contrast_examples.en: Mogi (as the ongoing topic) didn't give up.

contrast_examples.jp: 茂木が勝った。
contrast_examples.en: It was Mogi who won (newly identified subject).

prompt.context_jp: 居間の宮沢___、テレビを見つめたまま しばらく身動きが取れなかった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 居間の宮沢___、テレビを見つめたまま しばらく身動きが取れなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that introduces Miyazawa as the topic of this paragraph.

feedback.correct_en: The narrator shifts the camera to Miyazawa in the living room — he becomes the topic the sentence will describe. は sets him as the frame; the comment follows.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would spotlight him as a newly identified actor, as if someone asked 'who couldn't move?' Here he is the lens, not the answer.

contrast_examples.jp: 宮沢は動けなかった。
contrast_examples.en: Miyazawa (topic) couldn't move.

contrast_examples.jp: 動けなくなったのは宮沢が最初だった。
contrast_examples.en: It was Miyazawa who first couldn't move.

prompt.context_jp: 宮沢の視線___、しかしその画面ではなく、別のどこかに向いていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 宮沢の視線___、しかしその画面ではなく…
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle given the contrastive 'しかし...ではなく' framing.

feedback.correct_en: しかし and ではなく set up an explicit contrast: everyone else is looking at the screen, but his gaze goes elsewhere. は naturally carries this contrastive nuance.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present 視線 as new focal info, missing the contrastive 'but as for his gaze...' structure the sentence is built on.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の視線は画面ではなく外に向いていた。
contrast_examples.en: His gaze (in contrast) was on the outside, not the screen.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の視線が急に動いた。
contrast_examples.en: His gaze suddenly moved (new event).

prompt.context_jp: 古参の富島の目___険しく、若手の安田___逆に前のめりだった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 古参の富島の目は険しく、若手の安田___逆に前のめりだった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits the parallel 'A vs B' contrast structure.

feedback.correct_en: The sentence contrasts the veteran Tomishima with the young Yasuda — explicitly flagged by 逆に. Parallel は...は... pairs are the standard way to express 'A is X, B on the other hand is Y.'
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make Yasuda a new focal subject rather than one half of a contrastive pair, breaking the A/B rhythm.

contrast_examples.jp: 父は厳しく、母は優しい。
contrast_examples.en: Father is strict; mother, on the other hand, is kind.

contrast_examples.jp: 父が怒った。
contrast_examples.en: It was father who got angry (new info).

prompt.context_jp:
「うちは足袋屋です 足袋だけじゃ いけませんか？」
富島の問い___、宮沢の胸に深く刺さった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 富島の問い___、宮沢の胸に深く刺さった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that connects back to the question just quoted.

feedback.correct_en: The 問い is already known — we just read it in the previous line. The narrator picks it up as the topic ('as for Tomishima's question, it struck him deeply'). は is natural for referring back.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would introduce 問い as new information, but it's the very question we just heard — it isn't new to us or to Miyazawa.

contrast_examples.jp: その言葉は胸に刺さった。
contrast_examples.en: Those (already-known) words pierced his heart.

contrast_examples.jp: 鋭い言葉が飛んできた。
contrast_examples.en: A sharp remark (new) came flying.

prompt.context_jp: 宮沢の声___、ふいに大きくなった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 宮沢の声___、ふいに大きくなった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for this sudden change.

feedback.correct_en: ふいに ('suddenly') signals a surprise event that everyone in the room notices in the moment. が spotlights 声 as the newly-occurring focal change.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame 声 as a continuing topic, which clashes with the abrupt, event-marking ふいに.

contrast_examples.jp: 声が急に大きくなった。
contrast_examples.en: His voice suddenly grew louder (new event).

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の声はいつも大きい。
contrast_examples.en: His voice (as topic) is always loud.

prompt.context_jp: 宮沢の足に、こはぜ屋の技術が結晶した一足___滑り込む。
prompt.prompt_jp: こはぜ屋の技術が結晶した一足___滑り込む。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle introducing the prototype shoe entering the scene.

feedback.correct_en: This is the dramatic reveal of the first prototype — it enters the scene for the first time. が marks the newly introduced subject of 滑り込む.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would wrongly treat the shoe as an established topic. を is wrong because 滑り込む here is intransitive — the shoe is slipping onto the foot, not being slipped by someone.

contrast_examples.jp: 一足のシューズが現れた。
contrast_examples.en: A pair of shoes appeared (newly introduced).

contrast_examples.jp: そのシューズはすぐ売れた。
contrast_examples.en: Those shoes (already known) sold out quickly.

prompt.context_jp:
「うちは たった… 20人の会社ですよ！」
宮沢の声___、応接室に響いた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 宮沢の声___、応接室に響いた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for this dramatic eruption.

feedback.correct_en: The sudden outburst echoing through the room is a new, dramatic event. が spotlights the声 as the focal subject of that occurrence.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn this into a general statement about his voice as a known topic, deflating the moment-of-event feel the narrator wants.

contrast_examples.jp: 怒鳴り声が響いた。
contrast_examples.en: A shout rang out (new event).

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の声は低い。
contrast_examples.en: His voice (as topic) is low.

prompt.context_jp: 宮沢___作業場に姿を現した。
prompt.prompt_jp: 宮沢___作業場に姿を現した。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle introducing Miyazawa's entrance to the scene.

feedback.correct_en: The workers were just talking among themselves — Miyazawa newly appears on scene. 姿を現す is a classic 'enter the stage' event that takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would already presuppose him as the topic being discussed, but the paragraph pivots to his arrival as a new beat.

contrast_examples.jp: 社長が現れた。
contrast_examples.en: The president appeared (new entrance).

contrast_examples.jp: 社長はまだ来ない。
contrast_examples.en: The president (as topic) hasn't come yet.

prompt.context_jp: 足の裏から突き上げる痛みに、彼の顔___蒼白だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼の顔___蒼白だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle describing an attribute of the already-known subject.

feedback.correct_en: The focus is on Mogi (established topic); the sentence predicates a state about him via 顔. は is natural for 'as for his face, it was pale' — describing a known subject.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would pick 顔 out as newly identified ('it was his face that was pale'), which doesn't fit the flowing description of his known suffering.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の顔は青かった。
contrast_examples.en: His face was pale (describing the known subject).

contrast_examples.jp: 青ざめた顔が印象的だった。
contrast_examples.en: His pale face (newly focal) was striking.

prompt.context_jp: 先細る足袋事業と、怪我に苦しむランナーの姿___、彼の中で一本の線につながろうとしていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 〜ランナーの姿___、彼の中で一本の線につながろうとしていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle inside this subordinate clause with a complex subject.

feedback.correct_en: This is a descriptive sentence introducing two things that newly connect in Miyazawa's mind. The compound subject '先細る足袋事業と…ランナーの姿' is the focal new idea; が marks it.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would elevate this long noun phrase to global topic status, but the sentence is describing a dawning realization, not commenting on a known theme.

contrast_examples.jp: 二つの点が一本の線につながった。
contrast_examples.en: Two points connected into a line (new observation).

contrast_examples.jp: その二つは関係ない。
contrast_examples.en: Those two (known) are unrelated.

prompt.context_jp: 先頭集団に食らいつく彼の走りには、勝つか、諦めるか、どちらかしかないという___ものが漂っていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 勝つか、諦めるか、どちらかしかないという___ものが漂っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the expression that describes an intense, almost frightening aura.

feedback.correct_en: 鬼気迫る literally 'oni-energy closing in' — a chilling, do-or-die intensity. Perfect for a runner with only 'win or quit' showing in his back.
feedback.incorrect_en: 心温まる ('heartwarming') is positive and gentle; のほほんとした ('carefree') is the opposite of intense. Neither fits the win-or-quit atmosphere.

contrast_examples.jp: 鬼気迫る表情で机に向かう。
contrast_examples.en: He faces the desk with a chilling intensity.

contrast_examples.jp: 心温まるエピソード。
contrast_examples.en: A heartwarming anecdote.

prompt.context_jp: 痛みに___、また身体が傾く。
prompt.prompt_jp: 痛みに___、また身体が傾く。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the verb form meaning 'unable to bear.'

feedback.correct_en: 〜かねる means 'cannot (bring oneself to) do.' 耐えかねて captures Mogi reaching the limit of what his body can endure.
feedback.incorrect_en: 耐えすぎて ('bearing too much') is ungrammatical in this reading; 耐えたくて ('wanting to endure') describes desire, not inability.

contrast_examples.jp: 見るに耐えかねて目をそらした。
contrast_examples.en: Unable to bear watching, he looked away.

contrast_examples.jp: 我慢しすぎて体を壊す。
contrast_examples.en: He ruins his health by enduring too much.

prompt.context_jp: 大地の反対を___、宮沢は自分の中で決意を固めていった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 大地の反対を___、宮沢は自分の中で決意を固めていった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the verb meaning 'to let (someone's words) pass without responding.'

feedback.correct_en: 聞き流す = hear-and-let-flow, i.e. let it pass without taking it in. Miyazawa quietly ignores Daichi's protest and strengthens his resolve.
feedback.incorrect_en: 聞き入れる means 'accept/grant,' the opposite of what Miyazawa does. 聞き返す means 'ask back,' which doesn't fit either.

contrast_examples.jp: 文句を聞き流す。
contrast_examples.en: Let the complaints wash over you.

contrast_examples.jp: 要望を聞き入れる。
contrast_examples.en: Grant someone's request.

prompt.context_jp: 富島の問いは、宮沢の胸に深く___。
prompt.prompt_jp: 富島の問いは、宮沢の胸に深く___。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the verb that collocates with words 'piercing' the heart.

feedback.correct_en: 胸に刺さる is the set collocation for painful words that lodge deep inside you. Tomishima's question hits Miyazawa right where it hurts.
feedback.incorrect_en: 胸に落ちる means 'to be understood/accepted,' a calm realization. 胸に入る is not idiomatic for emotional impact.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の言葉が胸に刺さった。
contrast_examples.en: His words pierced my heart.

contrast_examples.jp: ようやく胸に落ちた。
contrast_examples.en: It finally sank in / made sense.

prompt.context_jp: 彼の中で長年___焦りが、はじめて言葉となって噴き出した瞬間だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼の中で長年___焦りが、はじめて言葉となって噴き出した。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the verb for feelings that smolder quietly inside for years.

feedback.correct_en: くすぶる = smolder: a slow, suppressed burning that doesn't flare up. Perfect for anxiety that's been quietly building for years before erupting into words.
feedback.incorrect_en: 燃え尽きた ('burned out') means already extinguished — contradicting 噴き出した. 吹き飛んだ ('blown away') is also the wrong direction.

contrast_examples.jp: 不満が心の中でくすぶる。
contrast_examples.en: Discontent smolders in one's heart.

contrast_examples.jp: 情熱が燃え尽きる。
contrast_examples.en: One's passion burns out.

prompt.context_jp: ___口調に、宮沢は背筋を伸ばして向き合う。
prompt.prompt_jp: ___口調に、宮沢は背筋を伸ばして向き合う。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the expression describing rapid-fire, pressing speech.

feedback.correct_en: 畳みかける = press one's point rapidly without letting the other side respond. Fits the hard-talking Kansai bank executive who's bearing down on Miyazawa.
feedback.incorrect_en: とろけるような ('melting') and 眠たげな ('drowsy') suggest soft or sleepy delivery — the opposite of a bank executive on the offensive.

contrast_examples.jp: 畳みかけるように質問する。
contrast_examples.en: Fire off questions one after another.

contrast_examples.jp: とろけるような声でささやく。
contrast_examples.en: Whisper in a melting voice.

prompt.context_jp: それで最大の売りは 足袋ならではの 軽さとフィット感のある ___の靴
prompt.prompt_jp: 足袋ならではの 軽さとフィット感のある ___の靴
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the concept phrase that became Kohaze-ya's design slogan.

feedback.correct_en: 裸足感覚 ('a barefoot sensation') is the concept the team settles on — light, close-fitting, letting you feel the ground. The next line even echoes it: 「裸足感覚」.
feedback.incorrect_en: 重量感 (heavy feel) and 高級感 (upscale feel) are both marketing clichés that clash with the lightweight tabi-style design.

contrast_examples.jp: 裸足感覚のランニングシューズ。
contrast_examples.en: Running shoes with a barefoot feel.

contrast_examples.jp: 高級感のある革靴。
contrast_examples.en: Leather shoes with an upscale feel.

prompt.context_jp: 努力ではどうにもならない壁があることを、彼は経営者として何度も___きていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼は経営者として何度も___きていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the verb meaning 'to taste / experience firsthand.'

feedback.correct_en: 味わう extends beyond food to mean 'experience deeply' — common for hardship, defeat, success. Miyazawa has 'tasted' these walls many times as a manager.
feedback.incorrect_en: 食べる and 飲む are literal eating/drinking; they don't take abstract objects like 'walls' or 'experiences.'

contrast_examples.jp: 挫折を味わう。
contrast_examples.en: To experience setback firsthand.

contrast_examples.jp: 成功の喜びを味わう。
contrast_examples.en: To savor the joy of success.

prompt.context_jp: Opening scene of the marathon broadcast.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds most natural as a narrative opening line?

choices.text: 豊橋国際マラソンの終盤、沿道の空気は張り詰めていた。
沿道の空気は張り詰めていた、豊橋国際マラソンの終盤に。
張り詰めていた、沿道の空気は豊橋国際マラソンの終盤。

feedback.correct_en: Japanese narrative prose puts time/place setters first, then the topic, then the predicate. 'When → where → what' is the standard flow of a scene opener.
feedback.incorrect_en: B tacks the time phrase on at the end, which reads like a spoken afterthought and is awkward in written narrative. C fronts the verb — grammatical only in poetry or emphatic inversion, not neutral prose.

contrast_examples.jp: 夜の街に、静かな風が吹いていた。
contrast_examples.en: In the night streets, a quiet wind was blowing.

contrast_examples.jp: 風が吹いていた、夜の街に。
contrast_examples.en: (Marked / afterthought order.)

prompt.context_jp: Miyazawa breaks the news to his son that he wants to try making running shoes.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds most natural as Miyazawa's announcement to Daichi?

choices.text: ランニングシューズを作ってみようと思う。
ランニングシューズを作ってみたいと思う。
ランニングシューズを作ろうと思っている考えだ。

feedback.correct_en: 〜てみようと思う ('I think I'll try doing...') is the natural, decisive way to voice a new plan. It conveys both intent and the exploratory 'give it a go' tone that fits a father announcing a bold decision.
feedback.incorrect_en: B weakens the resolve to a mere wish ('I'd like to try'). C stacks 思う on top of 考えだ redundantly — unnatural overlap of two 'thought' nouns.

contrast_examples.jp: 新しい仕事を始めてみようと思う。
contrast_examples.en: I think I'll try starting a new job.

contrast_examples.jp: 新しい仕事を始めたいと思う。
contrast_examples.en: I'd like to start a new job (weaker intent).

prompt.context_jp: Miyazawa tries on the first prototype and gives his verdict.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds most natural as the test-wearer's reaction?

choices.text: ぴったりだ。履き心地も悪くねえぞ。
ぴったりだ。履き心地も悪いじゃないよ。
ぴったりだ。履き心地も否定できない。

feedback.correct_en: 悪くない ('not bad' = pretty good) is the standard understated compliment. The 悪くねえぞ form adds a casual, masculine shop-floor tone that fits Miyazawa's register.
feedback.incorrect_en: B garbles the structure: 悪いじゃないよ doesn't idiomatically mean 'not bad.' C ('cannot be denied') sounds like a legal brief, not a shoe-fitting reaction.

contrast_examples.jp: この店、味も悪くないね。
contrast_examples.en: This place — the food's not bad either.

contrast_examples.jp: 味は否定できない。
contrast_examples.en: The flavor can't be denied (stilted / legalistic).

prompt.context_jp: When Ebata apologizes for being harsh, Miyazawa reassures him.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds most natural as Miyazawa's reply?

choices.text: ここで遠慮していいもんができなかったら意味がない。
ここで遠慮して、いいもんができなくても意味はある。
ここで遠慮されて、いいもんができたから意味がある。

feedback.correct_en: The logic 'if you hold back and we end up with a bad product, there's no point' matches both the story context and natural conditional phrasing (〜たら〜ない意味がない).
feedback.incorrect_en: B flips the meaning — Miyazawa isn't saying holding back is fine. C uses the passive 遠慮される strangely and reverses the point about honesty mattering.

contrast_examples.jp: ここで黙っていい結果が出なかったら意味がない。
contrast_examples.en: There's no point staying silent if it leads to a bad result.

contrast_examples.jp: 遠慮なく言ってください。
contrast_examples.en: Please speak without holding back.

prompt.context_jp: Alone with his wife, Miyazawa drops his boss-mode and admits his fear.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds most natural as his private confession?

choices.text: ホントは ちょっとビビってんだ。
実のところ、少々 畏怖の念を抱いております。
本当に ちょっと ビビっているのです。

feedback.correct_en: ビビってんだ (contraction of ビビっているんだ) is casual, confessional speech — exactly the stripped-down 'raw voice' tone the narrator describes.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is heavy keigo better suited to a formal speech, not a late-night husband-wife talk. C is grammatical but the 〜のです ending makes it stiffly explanatory, not intimate.

contrast_examples.jp: 正直、ちょっとビビってる。
contrast_examples.en: Honestly, I'm a little scared.

contrast_examples.jp: 畏怖の念を抱いております。
contrast_examples.en: I harbor a feeling of awe (formal).
